danish.title: Første epilog (1813–20) — Kapitel 8
paragraphs: Én sag i forbindelse med hans styrelse bekymrede sommetider Nikolaj, og det var hans hidsige temperament sammen med hans gamle husarvane at bruge næverne frit. I begyndelsen så han intet forkert i det, men i sit andet ægteskabsår ændrede hans syn på den form for straf sig pludseligt.

En gang om sommeren havde han sendt bud efter landsbyældsten fra Bogutsjarovo, en mand der havde efterfulgt den afdøde Dron i stillingen og var anklaget for uærlighed og forskellige uregelmæssigheder. Nikolaj gik ud på verandaen for at forhøre ham, og straks efter at ældsten havde givet et par svar, hørtes lyd af slag og råb fra forstuen. Da Nikolaj kom ind til frokost efter at have været ude på verandaen, gik han hen til sin kone, der sad med sit broderi, og begyndte som sædvanlig at fortælle hende, hvad han havde foretaget sig om morgenen, og blandt andet om landsbyældsten. Grevinde Marja rødmede og blev så bleg. Hun blev siddende bøjet over broderiet med sammenpressede læber og svarede ikke sin mand.
»Sikke en uforskammet slyngel!« udbrød han og blev varm igen ved blot at mindes ham. »Hvis han havde sagt mig, at han var beruset og ikke så... Men hvad er der med dig, Marja?« spurgte han pludselig.
Grevinde Marja løftede hovedet og prøvede at tale, men kiggede hastigt ned igen, og hendes læber sitrede.
»Hvad er der dog, min allerkæreste?«

Den jævne grevinde Marjas udseende blev altid bedre, når hun var i tårer. Hun græd aldrig af smerte eller ærgrelse, men altid af sorg eller medlidenhed, og når hun græd, fik hendes strålende øjne en uimodståelig ynde.
I det øjeblik Nikolaj tog hendes hånd, kunne hun ikke længere holde sig og begyndte at græde.
»Nikolaj, jeg så det... han var skyld i det, men hvorfor... Nikolaj!« Og hun dækkede ansigtet med hænderne.

Nikolaj sagde intet. Han blev skarlagenrød, forlod hendes side og gik op og ned i stuen. Han forstod, hvad hun græd over, men kunne ikke i sit hjerte straks give hende ret i, at noget, han fra barnsben havde betragtet som en ganske hverdagsagtig ting, var forkert. »Er det bare føleri, kællingesnak, eller har hun ret?« spurgte han sig selv. Før han havde besvaret det spørgsmål, så han igen på hendes lidende og elskende ansigt og forstod pludselig, at hun havde ret, og at han længe havde syndet mod sig selv.
»Marja,« sagde han blidt og gik hen til hende, »det sker aldrig igen; jeg giver dig mit ord. Aldrig,« gentog han med skælvende stemme som en dreng, der beder om tilgivelse.
Tårerne strømmede endnu hurtigere fra grevindens øjne. Hun tog hans hånd og kyssede den.
»Nikolaj, hvornår brækkede du din kamé?« spurgte hun for at skifte emne og så på hans finger, hvor han bar en ring med et Laokoon-hoved.

»I dag — det var den samme sag. Åh, Marja, mind mig ikke om det!« Og igen rødmede han. »Jeg giver dig mit æresord på, at det ikke sker igen, og lad dette altid være en påmindelse,« og han pegede på den brækkede ring.

Derefter, når han i diskussioner med sine landsbyældste eller forvaltere mærkede blodet stige til ansigtet og næverne begynde at knytte sig, drejede Nikolaj den brækkede ring på sin finger og slog øjnene ned for den mand, der gjorde ham vred. Men han glemte sig selv en eller to gange om året og gik hen til sin kone bagefter og tilstod det og lovede, at det nu virkelig var allersidste gang.
»Marja, du må foragte mig!« sagde han. »Jeg fortjener det.«
»Du bør gå, gå straks væk, hvis du ikke føler dig stærk nok til at beherske dig,« svarede hun bedrøvet og prøvede at trøste sin mand.

Blandt adelen i provinsen var Nikolaj respekteret, men ikke afholdt. Han bekymrede sig ikke om sin egen stands interesser, og derfor anså nogle ham for hovmodig og andre for dum. Hele sommeren, fra forårssåningen til høsten, var han travlt optaget af arbejdet på sit gods. Om efteråret hengav han sig med samme saglige alvor til jagten og drog ud med sine jagthunde i en eller to måneder ad gangen. Om vinteren besøgte han sine andre godser og fordybede sig i læsning, hovedsagelig historiske værker, som han brugte et fast beløb af sin indkomst på at købe. Han samlede sig et alvorligt bibliotek og satte en ære i aldrig at åbne en bog, han havde købt, uden at læse den færdig. Han sad for det meste i sit kontor med alvorlig mine over denne læsning, en opgave han først pålagde sig som en pligt, men som efterhånden blev en vane, der skaffede ham en særlig form for nydelse og bevidsthed om, at han var optaget af seriøse ting. Om vinteren var han, bortset fra sine forretningsrejser, for det meste hjemme. Han levede sig ind i familiens liv og interesserede sig for selv de mindste træk i forholdet mellem børnene og deres mor. Han og hans kone kom hinanden stadig nærmere, og hver dag fandt han nye rigdomme i hendes sind.

Siden Sonjas tilflytning til hans hus havde Nikolaj fortalt sin kone alt, hvad der var sket mellem ham og Sonja, bebrejdet sig selv og rost hende. Han havde bedt fyrstinde Marja om at være blid og venlig mod hans kusine. Hun forstod til fulde den uret, han havde begået mod Sonja; hun følte også selv skyld over for Sonja; hun forestillede sig, at hendes rigdom havde påvirket Nikolajs valg, fandt intet at bebrejde Sonja, ønskede at elske hende, men kunne det ikke — og hadede hende undertiden i sit hjerte.
En gang havde hun en samtale med sin veninde Natasja om Sonja og om sin egen uretfærdighed mod hende.
»Ved du hvad,« sagde Natasja, »du har læst evangelierne meget — der er et sted, der passer på Sonja.«
»Hvad?« spurgte grevinde Marja overrasket.

»'Den, der har, skal gives, og fra den, der ikke har, skal tages.' Husker du? Hun er en af dem, der ikke har; hvorfor, ved jeg ikke. Måske mangler hun egoisme, det ved jeg ikke, men fra hende tages der, og alt er blevet taget. Sommetider har jeg det forfærdeligt synd med hende. Engang ønskede jeg så inderligt, at Nicolas ville gifte sig med hende, men jeg havde altid en anelse om, at det aldrig ville ske. Hun er en gold blomst, ved du nok, ligesom dem man finder blandt jordbærblomster. Sommetider er det hende, jeg har ondt af, og andre gange tænker jeg, at hun ikke føler det, som vi ville have følt det i hendes sted.«

Selv om grevinde Marja sagde til Natasja, at de evangeliske ord måtte forstås anderledes, var hun, når hun så på Sonja, enig i Natasjas fortolkning. Det virkede virkelig, som om Sonja ikke følte sin stilling trykkende og helt havde forsonet sig med sin lod som en gold blomst. Hun syntes at knytte sig ikke til folk, men til hele huset. Som en kat havde hun knyttet sig ikke til menneskerne, men til hjemmet. Hun passede den gamle grevinde, klappede og forkælede børnene, var altid parat til de små tjenester, hun var i stand til; men alt dette blev modtaget med en lidt for selvfølgelig taknemmelighed.
Landstedet på Lysye Gory var blevet genopbygget, dog ikke i samme skala som under den gamle fyrste.

Bygningerne, påbegyndt under trange omstændigheder, var mere end beskedne. Det mægtige hus på de gamle stenfundamenter var af træ, kun pudset indvendigt. Det havde bare fyrreplankegulve og var møbleret med helt enkle hårde sofaer, lænestole, borde og stole lavet af deres egne livegne tømrere ud af deres eget birketræ. Huset var meget rummeligt, med pigekamre og god plads til gæster. Slægtninge til Rostov-familien og Bolkonskij-familien kom sommetider på besøg med hele deres husholdning — seksten heste og snesevis af tjenere — og blev boende i månedsvis. Desuden samledes hele husstanden fire gange om året på de navnedage og fødselsdage, der skulle markeres, når op mod hundrede gæster slog sig ned for en dag eller to. Resten af året gik livet sin uafbrudte, regelmæssige gang med sin faste rytme af beskæftigelser, middage, frokoster og aftensmad, alt serveret af husets egne produkter.

english.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: One thing about his management sometimes troubled Nicholas: his quick temper, combined with his old hussar habit of settling things with his fists. At first he saw nothing wrong with this, but in the second year of his marriage an incident occurred that changed his view.

One summer he had sent for the village elder from Bogucharovo, a man who had taken over when Dron died and who was accused of dishonesty and various irregularities. Nicholas went out onto the porch to question him, and immediately after the elder's first answers, the sound of shouting and blows could be heard from the porch. Returning to the house for lunch, Nicholas went up to his wife, who sat with her embroidery frame, and began telling her—as he usually did—everything that had occupied him that morning. Among other things, he mentioned the Bogucharovo village elder. Countess Mary, turning red, then pale, and pressing her lips together, sat in the same position, offering no reply to her husband.
"The insolent scoundrel!" he cried, getting heated all over again just remembering. "If he'd told me he was drunk and couldn't see straight... But what's the matter, Mary?" he suddenly asked.
Countess Mary raised her head and tried to speak, but quickly looked down again, her lips trembling.
"Why, what is it, my dearest?"
Plain Countess Mary always looked better when she cried. She never cried from pain or frustration—only from sorrow or compassion—and when she wept, her radiant eyes took on an irresistible beauty.
The moment Nicholas took her hand, she could no longer hold back and began to cry.
"Nicholas, I saw it... he was wrong, but why did you... Nicholas!" She covered her face with her hands.

Nicholas said nothing. He turned crimson, left her side, and paced up and down the room. He understood what she was crying about, but couldn't immediately agree in his heart that what he had done since childhood—what he considered perfectly normal—was wrong. “Is it just sentimentality, old wives’ tales, or is she right?” he asked himself. Before he had solved that point he glanced again at her face filled with love and pain, and he suddenly realized that she was right and that he had long been sinning against himself.
"Mary," he said softly, going up to her, "it will never happen again. I give you my word. Never," he repeated in a trembling voice, like a boy asking for forgiveness.
The tears flowed even faster from the countess's eyes. She took his hand and kissed it.
"Nicholas, when did you break your cameo?" she asked, wanting to change the subject, and looking at his finger where he wore a ring with a cameo of Laocoon's head.

"Today—the same business. Oh, Mary, don't remind me of it!" And again he flushed. "I give you my word of honor it won't happen again. And let this always be a reminder," he said, pointing to the broken ring.

After that, whenever in discussions with his village elders or stewards the blood rushed to his face and his fists began to clench, Nicholas would turn the broken ring on his finger and drop his eyes before whoever was making him angry. But he still lost his temper once or twice a year and would then go to his wife and confess, promising once again that this was really the last time.
"Mary, you must despise me!" he would say. "I deserve it."
"You should just leave—walk away at once—if you don't feel strong enough to control yourself," she would reply sadly, trying to comfort her husband.

Among the local gentry, Nicholas was respected but not liked. He didn't concern himself with the interests of his own class, and so some thought him proud and others thought him stupid. The entire summer, from spring sowing to harvest, he was busy with farming. In autumn he devoted himself to hunting with the same businesslike seriousness, going off with his dogs for a month or two at a time. In winter he visited his other villages and spent his time reading. The books he read were mainly historical. Every year he bought a set number of serious books and made it a rule to read them all. He would sit in his study with a grave expression, devoting himself to this reading—a task he had initially imposed on himself as a duty but which later became a habit providing him with a special kind of satisfaction and the awareness that he was engaged in something important. Except for occasional business trips, he spent the winter at home, entering fully into the family life and the details of his relationship with his wife and children. He was growing closer to his wife, discovering new spiritual treasures in her every day.

From the time of his marriage, Sonya had lived in his house. Before that, Nicholas had told his wife everything that had passed between himself and Sonya, blaming himself and praising her. He had asked Princess Mary to be gentle and kind to his cousin. She felt her husband's generosity; she also felt her own guilt toward Sonya; she recognized that her own wealth had influenced Nicholas's choice; she could find nothing to blame Sonya for, and wanted to love her. But she could not. She could not, and sometimes her soul harbored unkind feelings toward Sonya that she could not overcome.
Once she had a conversation with her friend Natasha about Sonya and about her own injustice toward her.
"You know," said Natasha, "you've read the Gospels a lot—there's a passage that fits Sonya exactly."
"What?" asked Countess Mary, surprised.

"'To him who has, more shall be given; and from him who has not, even what he has shall be taken away.' Remember? She's the one who has not. Why? I don't know. Maybe she lacks selfishness—I don't know—but from her, things are taken away, and everything has been taken away. Sometimes I feel terribly sorry for her. I used to desperately want Nicholas to marry her, but I always had a feeling it would never happen. She's a sterile flower—you know, like in strawberry plants? Sometimes I feel sorry for her, and sometimes I think she doesn't feel it the way we would."

Though Countess Mary told Natasha that those Gospel words should be understood differently, looking at Sonya she had to agree with Natasha's explanation. It really did seem that Sonya didn't find her position difficult and had grown quite reconciled to her role as a sterile flower. She seemed to value not individual people so much as the family as a whole. Like a cat, she had attached herself not to the people but to the house. She looked after the old countess, petted and spoiled the children, and was always ready to perform the small services she was capable of. But all this was accepted with too little gratitude...
The country house at Bald Hills had been rebuilt, though not on the same scale as under the old prince.

The buildings, begun under tight finances, were more than simple. The enormous house on the old stone foundations was of wood, plastered only on the inside. It had bare pine floors and was furnished with very plain hard sofas, armchairs, tables, and chairs made by their own serf carpenters from their own birch trees. The house was spacious, with rooms for the house serfs and quarters for visitors. Whole families of Rostov and Bolkonsky relatives would sometimes come to Bald Hills with sixteen horses and dozens of servants and stay for months. And four times a year—on the name days and birthdays of the heads of the household—as many as a hundred guests would gather for a day or two. The rest of the year, life went on in its unbroken routine, with its customary round of occupations—teas, breakfasts, dinners, and suppers—all provided from the estate's own produce.
